chapters.n: Leviticus picks up right where Exodus ends: God, now dwelling in the tabernacle, speaks to Moses from it. The book teaches Israel how a holy God and an imperfect people can live together.

f.g: The Hebrew title of Leviticus is Vayikra, “And he called.”

chapters.n: The first offering described is the burnt offering. Worshippers could bring cattle, sheep, or goats from their own herds — something of real value to them.

f.g: Hebrew qorban — something brought near; offerings were a way of drawing near to God.

f.w: of the herd, and of the flock

chapters.n: A bull for a burnt offering had to be male and without defect, offered freely at the tent’s entrance. Its perfection pointed to Christ, the Lamb without blemish.

f.g: Hebrew olah — “that which goes up,” since the whole animal rose in smoke.

chapters.n: Laying a hand on the animal’s head identified the worshipper with it — the animal died in his place. Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that such sacrifices were “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten.”

f.w: put his hand upon the head

chapters.n: The worshipper himself killed the animal before the Lord, and the priests splashed its blood around the altar. Life is in the blood, so blood represents a life given.
The animal was skinned and cut into pieces. The priest kept the hide.
The priests kept the altar fire going and arranged the wood.
The pieces, including the head and fat, were placed on the fire.
After washing the entrails and legs, the priest burned the whole animal. Nothing was held back — a picture of complete devotion. God accepted it as a “sweet savour,” a pleasing aroma.

f.g: Pleasing aroma — the offering was accepted.

chapters.n: Those who could not afford a bull could bring a flawless male sheep or goat.
The animal was killed on the north side of the altar and its blood splashed on the altar.

f.g: The north side of the altar was the place of slaughter.

chapters.n: It was cut up and arranged on the fire like the bull.
After washing, the whole animal was burned as an offering pleasing to God. The same acceptance came whether the gift was large or small.
Even the poor could offer: two kinds of inexpensive birds were accepted. Mary and Joseph brought such birds after Jesus’s birth, showing their humble means.
Because a bird was small, the priest handled the entire offering, wringing off its head and draining the blood at the altar.
The crop and feathers were removed and thrown on the ash heap east of the altar.

f.g: The pouch in a bird’s throat for food.

chapters.n: The bird was torn open by the wings without being fully divided and burned whole. Even the poorest person’s humble gift was “a sweet savour unto the LORD” — God values the heart behind the offering.
The second offering is the grain offering — fine flour with olive oil and frankincense. It offered to God the fruit of one’s daily labor, acknowledging Him as the giver of daily bread.

f.g: Grain offering. In KJV English “meat” means food generally, not flesh; Hebrew minḥah, “gift” or “tribute.”

chapters.n: The priest burned a handful with all the frankincense as a “memorial” — a token portion representing the whole gift, as if to bring the worshipper to God’s remembrance.
The rest of the grain belonged to the priests as their food. It was “most holy” and had to be eaten in a holy place.
Grain offerings could also be baked — as thick cakes mixed with oil or thin wafers brushed with oil — but always without yeast.
Or it could be cooked on a flat griddle, again unleavened and mixed with oil.
The griddle-cake was broken into pieces with oil poured over it.
A third method used a covered pan, perhaps producing something like a dumpling cooked in oil.
However prepared, the offering was brought to the priest, who took it to the altar.
The priest burned a token portion, pleasing to the Lord.
The rest was given to the priests, who served at the altar and lived from these offerings.
No yeast or honey could be burned on the altar, possibly because both cause fermentation and decay — fitting symbols of corruption.

f.g: Yeast or sourdough; often a symbol of sin or corruption.
Possibly any sweet fruit syrup, such as date honey.

chapters.n: Leaven and honey could be given among the firstfruits to the priests, but not burned on the altar.

f.g: The first and best of the harvest.

chapters.n: Every grain offering had to include salt, called “the salt of the covenant.” Salt preserves and does not decay, symbolizing a lasting, unbreakable covenant. Jesus called His disciples “the salt of the earth.”
A firstfruits grain offering used fresh heads of grain roasted over fire and crushed.

f.g: Fresh heads of grain (wheat or barley), not maize.
Crushed or coarsely ground new grain.

chapters.n: Oil and frankincense were added as with other grain offerings.
The priest burned a token portion with all the frankincense. Giving God the first of the harvest showed trust that He would provide the rest.

The third type is the peace offering, a fellowship sacrifice shared between God, the priest, and the worshipper, who ate most of it in a joyful meal. Unlike the burnt offering, male or female animals were allowed.

f.g: Hebrew shelamim, from shalom — peace, wholeness, being at one with God.

chapters.n: As with the burnt offering, the worshipper laid his hand on the animal and killed it, and the priests splashed its blood on the altar. Peace with God comes through atonement first.

f.w: lay his hand upon the head

chapters.n: God’s portion was the fat around the internal organs — the richest part, considered the best.
Also burned were the kidneys and the fatty lobe of the liver. In Hebrew thought the kidneys were linked to a person’s innermost feelings.

f.g: The fatty lobe covering the liver.

chapters.n: The fat was burned on top of the daily burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the Lord.
A sheep or goat from the flock could also be a peace offering, male or female, without defect.
If the offering was a lamb, it was presented before the Lord.
The same procedure followed: hand on its head, slaughter at the tent, blood on the altar.
For a sheep, the large fat tail was included in God’s portion, removed close to the backbone along with the fat of the organs.

f.g: The broad fat tail of Middle Eastern sheep, considered a delicacy.

chapters.n: The kidneys and liver lobe were removed as with cattle.
The priest burned these as “the food of the offering” — language of a shared meal, as if God were dining with His people.

f.g: Literally “bread” — the offering is pictured as God’s portion of a shared meal.

chapters.n: A goat could also be given as a peace offering.
The same steps: hand on its head, slaughter at the tent, blood on the altar.
The fat of the inner organs was again given to the Lord.
The kidneys and liver lobe were taken as well.
All the fat belongs to the Lord. Giving Him the best portion acknowledged Him as the source of all good things.

f.w: all the fat is the LORD's

chapters.n: Israel was forever forbidden to eat fat or blood. Blood represents life, which belongs to God; it is the means of atonement and must be treated as sacred.
The Lord now introduces the sin offering, for cleansing from sins committed without full awareness. Even unintended wrongs needed to be dealt with before a holy God.
This offering covers sins “through ignorance” — unintentional mistakes, or wrongs done without realizing it. Deliberate, defiant sin was treated differently.
The first case is the anointed high priest. Because his sin brought guilt on the people he represented, he had to offer the most valuable animal: a young bull.

f.g: Hebrew ḥattat — an offering that purifies from sin.

chapters.n: He brings the bull to the tent entrance, lays his hand on its head, and kills it before the Lord.

f.w: lay his hand upon the bullock's head

chapters.n: Unlike other offerings, the blood of this sacrifice was carried inside the tent itself, because the high priest’s sin had defiled the sanctuary.
He sprinkled the blood seven times before the veil. Seven, the number of completeness, signaled full cleansing.
Blood went on the horns of the incense altar inside, and the rest was poured at the base of the outer altar.

f.w: horns of the altar of sweet incense

chapters.n: All the fat was removed, as with the peace offering.
The kidneys and the fatty lobe of the liver were also removed.
These fat portions were burned on the outer altar, as in the peace offering.
Everything else — hide, meat, head, legs, organs, and dung — was not eaten by anyone.
The entire remainder was carried outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place and burned. Hebrews sees Jesus, who “suffered without the gate,” in this image.
Next, if the whole community sins unknowingly and the matter is hidden from them, they become guilty as a nation.
Once the sin becomes known, the community must bring a young bull, the same costly offering as the high priest’s.
The elders, representing the whole people, lay their hands on its head.
The high priest carries its blood into the tent of meeting.
He sprinkles the blood seven times before the veil.
Blood goes on the incense altar’s horns and the rest is poured at the base of the outer altar.
All the fat is burned on the altar.
The priest follows the same procedure as for the high priest’s bull, making atonement — and the promise is clear: “it shall be forgiven them.”

f.g: Hebrew kipper — to cover, purge, or reconcile.

chapters.n: The bull is burned outside the camp, as the first one was.
Third, if a tribal leader unknowingly breaks a command and becomes guilty, he too must bring an offering.
Once he realizes his sin, he brings a male goat — less costly than a bull, reflecting his lesser role.
He lays his hand on it and kills it where burnt offerings are slaughtered.
For leaders and common people, the blood went only on the outer altar’s horns, not inside the tent.
The fat is burned and the leader is forgiven. Higher position meant greater responsibility, but forgiveness was available to all.
Fourth, any ordinary Israelite who unknowingly sins becomes guilty.

f.g: Literally “people of the land” — ordinary citizens.

chapters.n: When he becomes aware, he brings a female goat without defect.
He lays his hand on it and slays it at the place of burnt offering.
The priest puts blood on the outer altar’s horns and pours out the rest.
The fat is burned as a pleasing aroma, and the person is forgiven. Even an ordinary person’s confession matters deeply to God.
An ordinary person could alternatively bring a female lamb.
He lays his hand on it and slays it as a sin offering.
The priest puts blood on the altar’s horns and pours the rest at its base.
The fat is burned, atonement is made, and the person is forgiven. Every level of society — priest, nation, leader, individual — had a path back to God.
Specific cases now follow. If someone hears a public call for witnesses under oath and stays silent about what he knows, he carries guilt. Withholding the truth can be a sin.

f.g: A public adjuration — a solemn call for witnesses to testify.
Carry the guilt and its consequences.

chapters.n: Touching the carcass of an unclean animal made a person ritually unclean, even if he did not notice at the time.

f.g: Ritually impure — unfit to approach holy things, not necessarily sinful.

chapters.n: Contact with human sources of impurity also defiled a person, and once he became aware of it, he was responsible to deal with it.
A rash, thoughtless oath — whether to do harm or good — also created guilt once the person realized what he had said. Words spoken lightly still matter to God.
In each case the person must confess the specific sin. Honest confession was a required step, not just the sacrifice.
Then he brought a female lamb or goat as a sin offering, and the priest made atonement for him.

f.g: Here used loosely for the penalty or guilt offering; Hebrew asham, “guilt.”

chapters.n: God made room for the poor: if someone could not afford a lamb, two doves or pigeons would do, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering.

f.w: two turtledoves, or two young pigeons

chapters.n: The priest offered the sin offering bird first, wringing its neck without severing the head completely.
Some of its blood was sprinkled on the side of the altar and the rest drained at the base.
The second bird was burned as a burnt offering, and the person was forgiven. Cleansing (sin offering) comes first, then dedication (burnt offering).
For the very poorest, even birds could be replaced by about two quarts of flour. No one was too poor to receive atonement. Because this was for sin, it lacked the joyful oil and frankincense.

f.g: About two quarts or two liters.

f.w: he shall put no oil upon it

chapters.n: The priest burned a handful as a token portion on the altar.
Atonement was made, the sin forgiven, and the remaining flour went to the priest. Grace was within reach of every Israelite.
The Lord now introduces the trespass (guilt) offering, for wrongs that caused loss to God or to others.
If someone accidentally misused something holy — for instance, failing to give tithes or offerings due to God — he had to bring a ram worth a set value in silver.

f.g: Things dedicated to God, such as tithes, firstfruits, or priestly portions.
A valuation set by the priest.

chapters.n: He also had to repay the loss plus one fifth more. Repentance included making things right, not just saying sorry.
Even when someone broke a commandment without realizing it, he was still guilty. Ignorance lessens culpability but does not erase the harm done.
He brought a flawless ram valued by the priest, and his error was atoned and forgiven.
The chapter closes by stressing the point: even an unintended wrong is a real trespass against the Lord, needing atonement.
The Lord continues teaching about the trespass offering, now for deliberate wrongs against a neighbor. (In Hebrew Bibles, verses 1–7 are counted as the end of chapter 5.)
Cheating a neighbor — lying about goods held in trust, a business deal, robbery, or extortion — is called a trespass “against the LORD.” Wronging others is wronging God.

f.g: In a pledge or business partnership.

chapters.n: Keeping a lost item you found and lying about it under oath is also included. Dishonesty in small things still breaks faith with God.
Once guilty, the offender must return whatever he took — stolen goods, entrusted property, or found items.
He repays the full amount plus 20 percent, on the same day he brings his offering. Reconciliation with one’s neighbor comes before reconciliation at the altar.
He then brings a flawless ram, valued by the priest, as a guilt offering.
The priest makes atonement and the sin is forgiven. Restitution plus sacrifice brought full restoration.
The Lord now gives instructions specifically for the priests about handling each offering.
The burnt offering was to stay on the altar burning all night until morning, with the altar fire kept alive.
In his linen garments, the priest removed the ashes each morning and set them beside the altar. Even cleaning up was sacred work done in holy clothing.
He then changed into ordinary clothes to carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place.
The altar fire must never go out. Every morning the priest added wood and offered sacrifices on it.

f.w: lay the burnt offering in order

chapters.n: “The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar” — a symbol of constant devotion. Many apply it to keeping one’s own spiritual fire alive.
Next are rules for the grain offering, presented by the priests at the altar.
A handful with all the frankincense was burned as the token portion.
The priests ate the rest without leaven, in the tabernacle courtyard. Holy food was eaten in a holy place.

f.g: Here, the courtyard of the tabernacle.

chapters.n: It was not to be baked with yeast. God calls it His gift to the priests — “most holy,” like the sin and trespass offerings.
Only male priests of Aaron’s family could eat it, and anything that touched it became holy.

f.w: every one that toucheth them shall be holy

chapters.n: The Lord gives a further instruction for the priests.
On the day a high priest was anointed (and, it seems, daily afterward), he offered a grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening.
It was cooked on a griddle with oil, broken into pieces, and offered as a pleasing aroma.
Each new high priest would continue this offering. It was burned entirely.

f.g: In his place, as his successor.

chapters.n: A priest’s own grain offering was never eaten — he could not benefit from his own offering, unlike offerings brought by the people.
The Lord turns to the sin offering’s regulations.
The sin offering was slaughtered in the same place as the burnt offering, and it was “most holy.”
The officiating priest ate it in the courtyard, a sign that the sin had been dealt with and the offering accepted.
Its holiness was contagious: anything touching it became holy, and any garment spattered with its blood had to be washed in the holy place.
Clay pots used to boil it were broken, and bronze pots were scoured, so the holy did not mix with the common.

f.g: Clay pot, porous and impossible to clean fully.

chapters.n: Any male priest could share in eating it, for it was most holy.
But when a sin offering’s blood was brought inside the tent (as for the high priest or the whole nation), its meat was burned, not eaten.

f.w: shall be burnt in the fire

chapters.n: The priests’ instructions continue with the trespass (guilt) offering, which, like the sin offering, is “most holy.”
It is slaughtered where the burnt offering is killed, and its blood is splashed around the altar rather than placed on the horns.
All its fat, including the fat tail, is offered to the Lord.

f.g: The fat tail of a sheep.

chapters.n: The kidneys and liver lobe are removed as in other offerings.
The priest burns these on the altar as a trespass offering to the Lord.
The meat goes to the male priests, eaten only in the holy place.
Sin and trespass offerings follow one rule: the officiating priest receives the meat. Those who serve at the altar are supported by it.
For burnt offerings, which were wholly burned, the priest received the hide.
Grain offerings cooked in an oven, covered pan, or griddle went to the officiating priest.
Uncooked grain offerings, with or without oil, were shared equally among all the priests.
Now come the rules for peace offerings, the fellowship sacrifices eaten by the worshipper.
A peace offering given for thanksgiving was accompanied by several kinds of unleavened bread.

f.g: An offering expressing gratitude for God’s help.
Well mixed, or soaked in oil.

chapters.n: Leavened bread was also included. Since it was eaten rather than burned on the altar, it was allowed here.
One of each kind of bread was given to the officiating priest as a contribution to the Lord.

f.g: A portion lifted up and set aside for God, then given to the priest.

chapters.n: Thanksgiving meat had to be eaten the same day — encouraging the worshipper to invite family and friends, especially the poor, to share the feast.

f.w: shall be eaten the same day

chapters.n: Offerings made to fulfill a vow or given freely could be eaten over two days.
Anything left on the third day had to be burned.
Eating it on the third day made the whole offering unacceptable and brought guilt. Holy food could not be treated carelessly as leftovers.
Meat that touched anything unclean had to be burned; otherwise, any clean person could eat it.
Eating holy meat while ritually unclean was serious: the person would be cut off from Israel.

f.g: Removed from the covenant community, possibly by divine judgment.

chapters.n: Touching an unclean person, animal, or object and then eating holy meat carried the same penalty. Approaching sacred things required preparation.

f.g: Detestable thing, such as an unclean creature.

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses further instructions for all Israel.
Israelites were not to eat the fat of cattle, sheep, or goats — the kinds of animals used for sacrifice.
Fat from animals that died naturally or were killed by predators could be used for other purposes, but never eaten.
Eating the fat of sacrificial animals meant being cut off, because that fat belonged to the Lord.
Blood of any bird or animal was never to be eaten, anywhere.
Eating blood also meant being cut off — blood, as the life, belonged to God alone.
The Lord speaks again to Moses.
Whoever offers a peace offering must bring the Lord’s portion personally.
The worshipper presented the fat and breast with his own hands; the breast was waved before the Lord. Worship was personal, not something handed off to others.

f.g: An offering moved before the altar in dedication to God.

chapters.n: The fat was burned, and the breast went to the priests.
The right thigh was also given to the priest as a contribution.

f.g: Probably the right thigh or leg.

chapters.n: The thigh belonged to the priest who offered the blood and fat.
God Himself takes the breast and thigh from Israel’s offerings and gives them to the priests permanently.

f.w: wave breast and the heave shoulder

chapters.n: This was the priests’ rightful share from the day they were anointed for service.

f.g: The share due to them because of their anointing.

chapters.n: God commanded Israel to give these portions to the priests forever.
A summary of the instructions for all the offerings: burnt, grain, sin, trespass, ordination, and peace offerings.

These laws came from the Lord to Moses at Sinai, when Israel was commanded to bring their offerings. Though the sacrifices ended with Christ’s Atonement, their meaning continues in a broken heart and a contrite spirit.
Now the narrative resumes. The Lord tells Moses to carry out the consecration of the priests that He commanded in Exodus 29.
Moses gathers everything needed: Aaron and his sons, the sacred garments, anointing oil, the animals, and the basket of bread.
The whole congregation is assembled at the tent entrance to witness the priests’ ordination. Sacred callings were conferred publicly, before the people.
Moses obeys, and the people gather at the entrance.
Moses explains to the people that what follows is commanded by the Lord, not his own invention.
First, Moses washes Aaron and his sons with water — a symbol of cleansing before sacred service.
Moses dresses Aaron in the tunic, sash, robe, and ephod with its woven band.
Then the breastplate, with the Urim and Thummim placed inside — instruments for receiving revelation for Israel.
Finally the turban with the golden plate, the “holy crown,” on its front.

f.g: The gold plate engraved “Holiness to the Lord.”

chapters.n: Moses anoints the tabernacle and everything inside it, setting it apart as holy.
He sprinkles the altar seven times and anoints it, its utensils, and the laver.
He pours anointing oil on Aaron’s head. The psalmist remembered this oil running down Aaron’s beard as an image of unity and blessing.

f.w: poured of the anointing oil upon Aaron's head

chapters.n: Aaron’s sons are clothed in tunics, sashes, and caps.
The sin offering bull is brought, and the priests lay their hands on its head, acknowledging their own need for atonement before serving others.

f.w: laid their hands upon the head

chapters.n: Moses applies the blood to the altar’s horns and pours the rest at its base, purifying and consecrating the altar for its work of reconciliation.
The fat and choice organs are burned on the altar.
The rest of the bull is burned outside the camp.
Next the ram for the burnt offering is brought, and the priests lay their hands on it.
It is killed and its blood splashed around the altar.
The ram is cut up and burned.
The whole ram is burned as a pleasing offering, symbolizing the priests’ total dedication to God.
Then the second ram, “the ram of consecration,” is brought, and hands are laid upon it.

f.g: Literally “ram of filling,” from the idiom for installing someone in office.

chapters.n: Moses puts its blood on Aaron’s right ear, thumb, and big toe — consecrating his hearing, his actions, and his walk to God’s service.
He does the same for Aaron’s sons and splashes the blood around the altar.
The fat portions and right thigh are taken.
One of each kind of bread is placed on top of them.
Moses places it all in the priests’ hands, and they wave it before the Lord. Their hands are literally “filled” as they are installed in office.

f.g: An offering presented by lifting it before the Lord.

chapters.n: Moses then burns these portions on the altar as an ordination offering.
Moses, acting as priest for this ceremony, receives the breast as his portion.
Moses sprinkles anointing oil and altar blood on the priests and their garments. Oil and blood together consecrate them — the Spirit and atonement working as one.
The priests are to boil the meat at the entrance and eat it with the bread — a sacred meal sealing their consecration.
Any leftover meat or bread must be burned.
The priests must remain at the tabernacle entrance for seven full days until their consecration is complete.
Everything done this day was commanded by the Lord to make atonement for them.
They must stay day and night for seven days and keep the Lord’s charge — sacred duty taken with utmost seriousness.

f.w: keep the charge of the LORD

f.g: A reminder that holy things require obedience.

chapters.n: Aaron and his sons did everything the Lord commanded through Moses. The chapter repeats “as the LORD commanded Moses” again and again, stressing exact obedience.
On the eighth day, after seven days of consecration, Aaron begins his ministry. The eighth day often signals a new beginning in scripture.
Aaron’s first act is to offer a sin offering and burnt offering for himself — a young calf, perhaps a quiet reminder of the golden calf he had made.
The people are to bring a goat for a sin offering and a calf and lamb for a burnt offering.
They also bring peace offerings and a grain offering, because “to day the LORD will appear unto you.” The whole service prepares for God’s presence.

f.w: to day the LORD will appear unto you

chapters.n: The people bring the offerings and gather before the Lord in expectation.
Moses promises that if they do what the Lord commanded, His glory will appear. Obedience prepares the way for God’s manifestation.

f.w: the glory of the LORD shall appear unto you

chapters.n: Aaron must first make atonement for himself, then for the people. A mediator must be clean before he can help others become clean — Christ alone needed no offering for Himself.
Aaron slays the calf of his own sin offering.
His sons bring the blood; he puts it on the horns of the altar and pours the rest at its base.
He burns the fat, kidneys, and liver lobe on the altar.
The meat and hide are burned outside the camp, as with sin offerings whose blood atoned for the priest.
Aaron offers his burnt offering, splashing its blood on the altar.
His sons hand him the pieces and head, and he burns them on the altar.
He washes the entrails and legs and burns them with the rest.
Then Aaron turns to the people’s offerings, slaying their goat as a sin offering just as he had done for himself.

f.g: As he did with his own sin offering.

chapters.n: He offers the people’s burnt offering according to the prescribed procedure.
He burns a handful of the grain offering in addition to the regular morning sacrifice.
He slays the bull and ram as peace offerings for the people and splashes their blood around the altar.
The fat portions of both animals are prepared for the altar.
The fat is laid on the breasts and then burned on the altar.
Aaron waves the breasts and right thigh before the Lord as the priests’ portion.
Having completed the offerings, Aaron raises his hands and blesses the people — perhaps with words like the priestly blessing in Numbers 6.
Moses and Aaron enter the tent together and come out to bless the people. Then the glory of the Lord appears to everyone — the promised goal of the whole day.

f.w: the glory of the LORD appeared unto all the people

chapters.n: Fire comes from the Lord’s presence and consumes the offering, showing that God accepts it. The people shout for joy and fall on their faces in worship.

f.w: there came a fire out from before the LORD

f.g: Bowed to the ground in awe and worship.

chapters.n: On the very day of glory, Aaron’s eldest sons Nadab and Abihu offer incense with “strange fire” — fire God had not authorized. The text stresses that they did what “he commanded them not.”

f.g: A pan for carrying hot coals and burning incense.
Unauthorized fire, perhaps not taken from the altar.

chapters.n: The same fire from the Lord that had just accepted the offerings now consumes them. God’s holiness, which blesses the obedient, is dangerous to those who treat it lightly.
Moses explains that God must be treated as holy by those who come close to Him. Those with greater access carry greater responsibility. Aaron, grieving, remains silent.

f.w: I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me

chapters.n: Moses calls two of Aaron’s cousins, Levites who were not priests, to carry the bodies out of the camp.
They carry the bodies away still in their priestly tunics — a sobering sight that the fire had killed them without burning their clothes.
Aaron and his surviving sons, still under their consecration, may not show the usual signs of mourning. The rest of Israel would mourn for them instead.

f.g: Do not let your hair hang loose, a sign of mourning.

chapters.n: They must remain at their sacred post because the anointing oil is on them. Their duty to God came before even their personal grief.
The Lord now speaks directly to Aaron — one of the few times He does so in Leviticus.
Priests must not drink wine or strong drink when serving in the tabernacle. Many have suggested Nadab and Abihu’s error was linked to drinking, though the text does not say so directly.

f.w: Do not drink wine nor strong drink

chapters.n: Priests needed clear minds to distinguish between holy and common, clean and unclean — the very distinctions taught in the chapters that follow.
Priests were also to be teachers, helping all Israel understand and keep the Lord’s laws.
Moses tells Aaron and his remaining sons to continue the service, eating the grain offering beside the altar as commanded.
It is their rightful portion and must be eaten in the holy place.
The breast and thigh of the peace offerings could be eaten by the priests’ whole families, including daughters, in any clean place.

f.g: A ritually pure location, not necessarily the sanctuary.

chapters.n: These portions belonged permanently to the priests and their families.
Moses discovers the people’s sin offering goat has been entirely burned instead of eaten by the priests, and he is angry.
Moses explains that eating the sin offering was part of how the priests bore the people’s guilt and made atonement.

f.w: to bear the iniquity of the congregation

chapters.n: Because its blood had not been taken inside the tent, the rules required the priests to eat it.

f.w: the blood of it was not brought in

chapters.n: Aaron responds humbly: after such a tragedy that day, would God have been pleased if he had eaten the holy offering? He seems to have felt unworthy to eat it while in such grief.

f.g: Such tragedy has happened to me.

chapters.n: Moses accepts Aaron’s explanation. God looks at the heart, and Aaron’s reverent motive was understood.
The Lord speaks to both Moses and Aaron, since priests would teach and apply these laws. Chapters 11–15 deal with “clean” and “unclean” — ritual purity needed to approach God.
God tells Israel which animals they may eat. These dietary rules (later called kosher laws) set Israel apart from other nations in everyday life.
Land animals were clean if they had fully split hooves and chewed the cud — cattle, sheep, goats, and deer, for example.

f.g: Has hooves divided into two parts.
Brings up and re-chews its food, as cows do.

chapters.n: Animals with only one of the two signs were unclean. The camel chews the cud but its foot is not truly split into hooves.
The coney, likely the rock hyrax, appears to chew its food like a ruminant but lacks hooves, so it was unclean.

f.g: Probably the rock hyrax, a small rabbit-sized animal of the region.

chapters.n: The hare moves its jaw as if chewing cud (and re-eats its own food), but has no hooves, so it was unclean.

f.g: The Bible describes animals by how they appear, not by modern biological categories.

chapters.n: Pigs have split hooves but do not chew the cud, so they were unclean. Avoiding pork became one of the most recognizable marks of Jewish identity.
Israelites were not to eat unclean animals or touch their carcasses.
Water creatures with both fins and scales — most ordinary fish — were clean.
Water creatures without fins and scales, such as shellfish and eels, were to be considered detestable.

f.g: Something detestable or to be avoided; here a ritual term, not necessarily moral evil.

chapters.n: Israel was to avoid eating them and to treat even their dead bodies as detestable.
The rule is repeated for emphasis: no fins and scales means unclean.
Next come forbidden birds — mostly birds of prey and scavengers that eat carrion or blood.

f.g: Possibly the black vulture or osprey; ancient bird names are uncertain.

chapters.n: Vultures and kites, scavengers and hunters, were unclean.

f.g: A bird of prey similar to a hawk.

chapters.n: Every kind of raven, which feeds on carrion, was unclean.
Owls, hawks, and other birds, some of uncertain identity, were also forbidden.

f.g: Probably a gull or sea bird; the identity is uncertain.
Uncertain; perhaps a type of owl.

chapters.n: Various owls and the cormorant, a fish-eating sea bird, were unclean.
The list continues with water birds and other scavengers.

f.g: Perhaps a kind of owl or water bird; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: Storks, herons, the hoopoe, and the bat (grouped with flying creatures) complete the list.

f.g: Listed with birds as a flying creature.

chapters.n: Most winged insects that walk on the ground were unclean.

f.g: An idiom for walking on the ground.

chapters.n: But winged insects with jointed legs for hopping were permitted.
Locusts and grasshoppers could be eaten. John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey.

f.g: Probably a type of cricket or locust.

chapters.n: All other winged insects that crawl were detestable.
Touching the carcass of an unclean animal made a person unclean until evening — a temporary condition, not a sin.

f.g: Until evening, when a new day began.

chapters.n: Carrying such a carcass required washing one’s clothes as well.
Animals with hooves that are not fully split, or that do not chew the cud, defile anyone who touches their carcasses.
Animals that walk on paws — like dogs, cats, and bears — were unclean, and touching their carcass caused uncleanness.
Carrying their carcass also required washing one’s clothes.
A special list of small creeping animals was unclean.

f.g: Probably a type of large lizard.

chapters.n: More small creatures, mostly lizards, completed this list.
Touching any of these when dead made a person unclean until evening.
Any household item that one of these dead creatures touched — wood, cloth, leather, or sacks — had to be washed and was unclean until evening.
Clay pots could not be thoroughly cleaned, so they had to be broken, and their contents became unclean.
Food or drink touched by water from such a vessel became unclean.
Clay ovens or stoves touched by a carcass also had to be broken down.
Springs and cisterns with plenty of water remained clean, a practical exception that protected vital water supplies, though the one who removed the carcass became unclean.
Dry seed for planting stayed clean even if touched by a carcass.
But seed that had been soaked in water became unclean if a carcass touched it — moisture was thought to transmit uncleanness.
Even a clean animal that died on its own made whoever touched its carcass unclean. Death itself was the opposite of the life God represents.
Eating or carrying such a carcass required washing clothes and waiting until evening.
Creatures that swarm or crawl on the ground were detestable and not to be eaten.
This included anything that slithers on its belly, walks on four legs close to the ground, or has many legs.
Israel must not defile themselves with these creatures.
Here is the heart of the chapter: “Be holy, for I am holy.” The food laws trained Israel to be different and to think of holiness in everyday choices. Peter quotes this verse to Christians.

f.w: ye shall be holy; for I am holy

chapters.n: God reminds them He freed them from Egypt to be their God. Holiness is a grateful response to redemption.

f.w: bringeth you up out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: A summary: this is the law concerning animals, birds, sea creatures, and creeping things.
Its purpose: to distinguish clean from unclean. The New Testament teaches that these food laws were fulfilled in Christ and are no longer binding.

f.w: the beast that may not be eaten

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses laws about a mother’s purification after childbirth. These are about ritual purity connected with blood and life, not about sin or the worth of mother or child.
After a son’s birth, a mother was ritually unclean for seven days, as during menstruation. Loss of blood — the symbol of life — brought temporary impurity.
On the eighth day the baby boy was circumcised, the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham. Jesus Himself was circumcised on the eighth day.

f.g: Removal of the foreskin, the covenant sign given to Abraham.

chapters.n: She then spent thirty-three more days in purification, not touching holy things or entering the sanctuary. This also gave the new mother a protected time of rest and recovery.

f.g: Anything holy, such as sacrificial food.

chapters.n: For a daughter, the periods were doubled: fourteen days, then sixty-six. The text does not explain why; scholars offer various suggestions, but none is certain.
When purification was complete, she brought a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a dove or pigeon for a sin offering. The sin offering here purified from ritual impurity, not from wrongdoing.
The priest offered them and made atonement, and she was declared clean. The same law applied for a son or a daughter.
A mother who could not afford a lamb could bring two birds instead. Mary, the mother of Jesus, brought this very offering of the poor at the temple.
The Lord gives Moses and Aaron detailed instructions for diagnosing skin diseases. The priest acted as a kind of public health inspector, protecting the community and the purity of the camp.
Any swelling, rash, or shiny spot that looked like a serious skin disease had to be shown to a priest. “Leprosy” in the Bible covers many skin conditions, not only modern Hansen’s disease.

f.g: Hebrew tsara‘at — a range of skin diseases (and even mold on cloth or walls), not necessarily modern leprosy.

chapters.n: If the hair in the sore had turned white and the sore went deeper than the skin, the priest declared it true tsara‘at and the person unclean.

f.w: in sight be deeper than the skin
f.g: Appears sunken below the surrounding skin.

chapters.n: If the signs were unclear, the person was isolated for seven days to see how the condition developed — a sensible quarantine.
If after a week the spot had not changed or spread, another seven-day quarantine followed. The priests were careful not to judge too quickly.
If after two weeks the spot was fading and not spreading, the person was declared clean. It was only a harmless rash; he washed his clothes and returned to normal life.
If the rash spread after being declared clean, he had to return to the priest.
If it was spreading, the priest declared it tsara‘at and the person unclean.
A second case: anyone with an apparent skin disease was brought to the priest for examination.
Signs included a white swelling, whitened hair, and raw open flesh in the swelling.

f.g: Live, raw flesh — an open sore.

chapters.n: These showed a chronic disease. No quarantine was needed; the person was simply unclean.
A surprising case follows: a condition that spreads over the entire body from head to foot.

If the whole body had turned white, the person was clean — likely because the condition had run its course and the skin was no longer raw. Some see a lesson: the one who fully acknowledges his condition is clean.
But if raw flesh appeared, the person became unclean.
Raw, open flesh was the key sign of active disease and uncleanness.
If the raw flesh healed and turned white again, he returned to the priest.
If healed, the priest declared him clean. The law always allowed for healing and restoration.
A third case concerns a boil that had healed.
If a white swelling or reddish-white spot appeared where the boil had been, it was shown to the priest.
If it was sunken and the hair white, it was tsara‘at breaking out of the old boil, and the person was unclean.
If there were no white hairs and it was not sunken but faded, a seven-day quarantine followed.
If it spread during that week, the person was unclean.
If it stayed the same, it was just the scar of the boil, and he was clean.
A fourth case concerns burns. A reddish or white spot might appear in a burn wound.
If the hair turned white and the spot was sunken, it was tsara‘at breaking out in the burn, and the person was unclean.
If there were no white hairs and it was not sunken but faded, a week of quarantine followed.
If it spread by the seventh day, the person was unclean.
If it did not spread and was faded, it was simply the scar of the burn, and the person was clean.
A fifth case concerns sores on the scalp or in the beard, for men or women.
If sunken with thin yellow hair, it was an itching scalp disease — a form of tsara‘at — and the person was unclean.

f.g: An itching, scaly disease of the scalp or beard.

chapters.n: If not sunken and without black hair, a week of quarantine followed.
On the seventh day the priest examined it again for spreading, yellow hair, or depth.
The person shaved around the sore (but not the sore itself) so the priest could watch its edges, and waited another week.
If it still had not spread, he was declared clean, washed his clothes, and was clean.
But if it spread after he was declared clean, he needed to be examined again.
If it was spreading, the priest did not need to look for yellow hair; spreading alone showed uncleanness.
If it stopped and healthy dark hair grew in it, the sore was healed and the person was clean.
A sixth case: white spots on the skin of a man or woman.
If they were dull white, it was a harmless rash, and the person was clean. Not every blemish disqualified someone.

f.g: A harmless skin rash, perhaps vitiligo or similar.

chapters.n: Simple baldness did not make a man unclean.
Baldness at the front of the head was likewise clean.

f.g: Bald at the front of the head.

chapters.n: But a reddish-white sore on a bald head could be tsara‘at.
The priest examined it to see if it looked like tsara‘at elsewhere on the body.
If so, the person was declared unclean because of the disease on his head.
A person with tsara‘at had to tear his clothes, let his hair hang loose, cover his upper lip, and call out “Unclean, unclean!” to warn others — outward signs of mourning and separation.
He lived alone outside the camp as long as the disease lasted. This isolation makes Jesus’s willingness to touch and heal lepers all the more striking.
The law now turns to tsara‘at in fabric — likely mold or mildew — in wool or linen garments.
It could appear in woven threads or in leather and leather goods.

f.g: The lengthwise and crosswise threads of woven cloth.

chapters.n: Greenish or reddish spots indicated the problem and had to be shown to the priest.
The priest set the item aside for seven days.
If the mark had spread, it was a destructive mold, and the item was unclean.
The contaminated item had to be burned to stop the spread.
If it had not spread after seven days, other steps were taken.
The item was washed and set aside another week.
If the spot did not change color after washing, even if it had not spread, the item was unclean and had to be burned.
If the spot faded after washing, the affected part was cut out.
If it reappeared, the item was burned.
If the washing removed it, the item was washed a second time and declared clean.

A summary of the law for mold in clothing and leather. The careful distinction between clean and unclean taught Israel that holiness reaches every part of life — and pointed to the need for a cleansing only God can give.
The Lord continues speaking to Moses at Sinai. Chapter 13 explained how to recognize skin disease; this chapter explains how a healed person is welcomed back.
This is the ritual for a person whose skin disease has already healed. The priest did not cure anyone; he confirmed the healing and restored the person to community and worship.

f.g: The Hebrew tsara‘at covered many skin conditions (and even mold on cloth or walls), not only what we now call leprosy.

chapters.n: The priest goes out to the person, because the unclean had to live outside the camp. Notice the movement: the representative of God goes out to meet the one who is shut out.
Four items are gathered: two clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop. Cedar resists decay, scarlet suggests blood and life, and hyssop was a common sprinkling plant.

f.g: A small bushy plant used as a sprinkling brush.
Yarn or cloth dyed bright red.

chapters.n: One bird is killed over fresh, flowing water held in a clay pot. “Running” water is literally “living water” in Hebrew, a picture of life and purity.
The living bird, along with the cedar, scarlet, and hyssop, is dipped into the blood and water. Life and death are joined in one act of cleansing.
The healed person is sprinkled seven times—a number of completeness—and declared clean. The living bird flies free, a vivid picture of the person’s release from their old condition.

f.g: Seven often signals wholeness or completion in Hebrew ritual.

chapters.n: The person washes, shaves, and bathes, then may enter the camp—but must stay outside their own tent for a week. Restoration happens in stages.
On the seventh day all hair is shaved again and another washing follows. The total shaving is like a fresh start, almost like a newborn.
On the eighth day come the temple offerings: lambs, flour mixed with oil, and a measure of olive oil. The eighth day often marks a new beginning in the law.

f.g: A “deal” is a portion; a tenth of an ephah, roughly two quarts or a couple of liters.
A log was a small liquid measure, a little over half a liter (about a pint).

chapters.n: The priest presents the person and the offerings at the tabernacle entrance. Someone once cut off now stands again “before the LORD.”
A trespass (guilt) offering comes first, waved with the oil before the Lord. The wave offering was lifted and moved toward the altar to show it was given to God.

f.g: An offering moved back and forth before the altar as a sign of dedication.

chapters.n: The lamb is slain in the sacred area where sin and burnt offerings were killed. Like the sin offering, its meat belongs to the priests and is “most holy.”
Blood is put on the person’s right ear, thumb, and big toe—exactly as when the priests were consecrated. The healed person is, in a sense, dedicated to hear, act, and walk for God.
The priest pours some oil into his own left palm, preparing for an anointing.
He sprinkles oil seven times toward the sanctuary, dedicating it to the Lord before using it on the person.
Oil is then placed on the same ear, thumb, and toe, over the blood. In scripture, blood often stands for cleansing and oil for consecration and the Spirit.
The rest of the oil is poured on the person’s head, like an anointing. The priest “makes an atonement”—covering and reconciling the person to God and the community.

f.g: Hebrew kipper, to cover, cleanse, or reconcile.

chapters.n: Next comes the sin offering, which dealt with impurity, followed by the burnt offering, a gift of full devotion.
The burnt and grain offerings complete the ritual, and the person is fully clean. The sequence—cleansing, then dedication—mirrors repentance followed by renewed commitment.

f.g: “Meat” here means food; this is the grain (flour) offering.

chapters.n: A merciful provision: if the person is poor, fewer animals are required. One lamb is still needed for the guilt offering, but the rest is reduced.
Birds may replace the second and third lambs. Mary and Joseph used this same poor person’s option at Jesus’s birth.

f.w: two turtledoves, or two young pigeons

chapters.n: The poor person comes on the same eighth day to the same holy place. Poverty never lowers anyone’s standing before God.
The ritual for the poor is otherwise identical: the lamb and oil are waved before the Lord.
Blood is again placed on right ear, thumb, and toe. The poor receive exactly the same consecration as the wealthy.
The priest again pours oil into his left palm.
He sprinkles it seven times before the Lord, as in verse 16.
The oil is placed over the blood on ear, thumb, and toe—the same anointing given to those with more means.
The remaining oil is put on the person’s head to make atonement. Every element of the full ritual is kept.
Whichever birds the person can afford become the remaining offerings.

f.g: Whatever he is able to obtain.

chapters.n: The phrase “such as he is able to get” repeats, stressing that God asks for what a person can honestly give.

f.w: Even such as he is able to get

chapters.n: A closing summary for the poor person’s cleansing.
A new topic begins, addressed to both Moses and Aaron: impurity in houses.
Looking ahead to life in Canaan, the Lord speaks of “plague” appearing in a house—likely mold, mildew, or fungus. Israel would live in stone houses instead of tents.

f.w: plague of leprosy in a house
f.g: Probably a spreading mold or fungus on walls.

chapters.n: The homeowner reports what looks like contamination. The priest serves as a kind of public health inspector.
Before inspection the house is emptied, so belongings are not declared unclean along with it. The law is practical and protects people’s property.
The priest looks for sunken, greenish or reddish streaks in the walls.
If suspicious, the house is closed for seven days to watch whether it spreads—like the waiting period for skin disease.
After a week the priest checks again to see whether the patches have spread.
If so, the infected stones are removed and dumped outside the city in a designated place.
The inside walls are scraped, and the scrapings are also carried away.
New stones and fresh plaster replace what was removed—repair before condemnation.
If the contamination returns after all this, a further inspection follows.
Spreading mold that keeps coming back is declared “fretting,” or destructive, and the house is unclean.
The whole house must be torn down and its materials removed. Some corruption must be cleared out completely rather than patched.
Anyone who enters the house while it is closed becomes unclean until evening.

f.g: even = evening; the new day began at sunset.

chapters.n: Sleeping or eating there requires washing one’s clothes.
If the replastered house stays clear, the priest declares it clean—the problem is “healed.”
Then a cleansing ritual like the one for a healed person is done for the house, with birds, cedar, scarlet, and hyssop.
One bird is killed over running water in a clay pot, as in verse 5.
The house is sprinkled seven times with the blood and water.
A list repeats every element used, emphasizing that the whole ritual has been completed.
The living bird is released into the fields, and atonement is made for the house. Even a home can be cleansed and dedicated to holy living.
The closing summary of chapters 13–14 begins: this is the law for all these conditions.

f.g: scall = a scaly, itchy scalp or skin condition

chapters.n: It covers contamination of garments and houses too.
Swellings, scabs, and bright spots are also included.
The purpose of these laws: to teach the difference between clean and unclean. Learning to distinguish is a theme throughout Leviticus.

f.w: To teach when it is unclean, and when it is clean

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses and Aaron laws about bodily discharges. These are about ritual purity—readiness to approach the sanctuary—not about sin or moral guilt.
An abnormal, ongoing discharge (probably an illness or infection) makes a man ritually unclean. Uncleanness was a temporary state that affected access to holy places.

f.g: A continual discharge from the body, likely from disease.
Ritually unfit to enter the sanctuary—not the same as sinful.

chapters.n: Whether the discharge is flowing or blocked, the condition counts as uncleanness while it lasts.
Beds and seats he uses also become unclean. Uncleanness was thought of as transferable by contact, a bit like contamination.
Touching his bed requires washing clothes, bathing, and waiting until evening. These rules also promoted good hygiene in a crowded camp.

f.g: Until evening, when a new day began.

chapters.n: Sitting where he sat brings the same short-term uncleanness.
Direct contact with his body also requires washing and waiting until evening.
Even being spat on by him calls for washing—another way the law guarded against spreading illness.
A saddle he rides on becomes unclean.
Anything that was under him, and anyone who carries such items, is unclean until evening.
If he touches someone without first rinsing his hands, that person must wash. Simple handwashing reduced the spread of uncleanness.
A clay pot he touches must be broken, since porous clay could not be fully cleaned; wooden vessels can be rinsed.
Once healed, he counts seven days, washes, and bathes in fresh “living” water to be clean.
On the eighth day he brings two inexpensive birds to the tabernacle—an offering anyone could afford.

f.g: Small doves; the least costly animal offering.

chapters.n: One bird is a sin offering, the other a burnt offering, and atonement is made. His restoration to worship is formally marked.

f.g: Here it means purifying and restoring, since no moral wrong is implied.

chapters.n: Normal emissions of semen bring a brief uncleanness that ends with bathing and evening. Life-giving processes were treated with reverence and distinguished from the holy sanctuary.
Clothing or leather touched by it is washed and unclean until evening.
After marital relations both husband and wife bathe and are unclean until evening. Intimacy in marriage was not sinful, but it was kept separate from temple worship.
A woman’s normal monthly period means seven days of separation. Those who touch her are unclean until evening; the rule concerns access to holy things, not her worth.

f.g: Set apart—ritually separate, not shamed or expelled.

chapters.n: Her bed and seat during this time become unclean.
Touching her bed means washing and waiting until evening.
So does touching anything she sat on.
Any item on her bed or seat also passes uncleanness to whoever touches it.
A man who has relations with her during her period is unclean for seven days. Leviticus 18:19 and 20:18 later forbid such relations outright.

f.w: if any man lie with her

chapters.n: If bleeding continues beyond the normal time, she remains unclean as long as it lasts. This describes the condition of the woman healed by Jesus after twelve years.

f.w: issue of her blood many days

chapters.n: During that prolonged condition, her bed and seat are treated as during her normal period.
Anyone touching those things washes and is unclean until evening.
When the bleeding stops, she counts seven days and is then clean.
On the eighth day she brings two doves or pigeons to the priest, just as the man did in verse 14.
Sin and burnt offerings restore her fully. Men and women are treated with the same pattern of cleansing.
The purpose: God’s dwelling is in the middle of Israel, so the people must keep it from defilement. Holiness requires care because God is truly present.

f.w: my tabernacle that is among them

chapters.n: A summary of the chapter’s laws for men begins.
The summary includes women and both normal and abnormal conditions, closing the section.
This chapter—the Day of Atonement—follows the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, who approached God carelessly. The Lord now shows the right way to come into His presence.

f.w: the death of the two sons of Aaron

chapters.n: Aaron may not enter the Most Holy Place whenever he likes. God’s presence appears in a cloud above the mercy seat, the lid of the ark, so entry is limited and reverent.

f.g: Behind the curtain separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
The gold lid of the ark of the covenant; Hebrew kapporet, related to kipper, “atone.”

chapters.n: Aaron must come prepared with a young bull for his own sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering.
Instead of his splendid robes, Aaron wears plain white linen and bathes first. On this day the high priest comes humbly, dressed simply, before God.

f.g: A simple white tunic, unlike the colorful high priestly garments of Exodus 28.

chapters.n: From the people he takes two male goats for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering. The goats represent the whole nation.
First Aaron offers the bull for himself and his household. Even the high priest needed atonement before he could act for others.

f.w: for himself, and for his house

chapters.n: The two goats are presented together at the tabernacle entrance.
Lots decide their roles: one for the Lord, one for “Azazel,” translated “scapegoat.” Casting lots left the choice in God’s hands.

f.g: Hebrew ‘aza’zel; often understood as “the goat that goes away.” Its exact meaning is debated.

chapters.n: The Lord’s goat becomes the sin offering for the people.
The scapegoat is kept alive and will be sent into the wilderness. Together the two goats picture both sides of atonement: sin paid for and sin carried away.

f.w: to let him go for a scapegoat into the wilderness

chapters.n: Aaron slaughters his own bull, completing the sacrifice for himself and his family.
He fills a censer with coals from the altar and takes handfuls of finely ground incense behind the veil.

f.g: A pan or firepan for carrying burning coals.

chapters.n: The incense smoke fills the room and veils the mercy seat, shielding Aaron as he stands in God’s presence. Incense often symbolizes prayer.

f.g: The tablets of the covenant kept inside the ark.

chapters.n: He sprinkles the bull’s blood on the mercy seat and seven times before it. Blood placed where God’s law rests shows that broken covenant is met with mercy.

f.w: sprinkle it with his finger upon the mercy seat

chapters.n: Then he kills the people’s goat and brings its blood behind the veil, doing the same. This was the only day anyone entered the Most Holy Place.

f.w: bring his blood within the veil

chapters.n: The sanctuary itself is cleansed from the impurity and sins of Israel, because God’s dwelling stands right in the middle of an imperfect people.

f.w: in the midst of their uncleanness
f.g: God chose to dwell among Israel despite their failings.

chapters.n: No one else may be in the tent while Aaron makes atonement. He alone stands between God and the people—a type of the one Mediator.

f.w: there shall be no man in the tabernacle

chapters.n: He goes out to the altar and puts blood from both bull and goat on its horns, cleansing it as well.

f.g: Horn-shaped projections on the altar’s corners.

chapters.n: Sprinkling the altar seven times cleanses and re-sanctifies it from a year of Israel’s impurity.
With the holy places reconciled, Aaron turns to the living goat.

f.g: Setting right; restoring a broken relationship.

chapters.n: Laying both hands on its head, Aaron confesses all Israel’s sins and places them on the goat. A designated man leads it away. Confession and transfer are the heart of this ritual.

f.w: lay both his hands upon the head

f.g: A man appointed or ready for the task.

chapters.n: The goat carries the people’s sins to an uninhabited land. Latter-day Saints see in this a picture of Jesus Christ, who bore our sins and carried them away.

f.w: bear upon him all their iniquities

chapters.n: Aaron returns to the tent, removes the linen garments, and leaves them there.
He bathes, puts on his regular high priestly garments, and offers the burnt offerings for himself and the people.
The fat of the sin offering is burned on the altar.
The man who led away the scapegoat must wash before reentering the camp, since he had been in contact with the sin-bearing goat.
The remains of the bull and goat are burned outside the camp. Hebrews links this to Jesus suffering “without the gate.”
The one who burns them also washes before returning.
This becomes a permanent yearly observance on the tenth day of the seventh month (Yom Kippur). “Afflict your souls” is usually understood as fasting and humbling oneself.
On this day the people are cleansed from all their sins before the Lord—the central promise of the day.
It is a solemn sabbath, a day of complete rest and humility before God.

f.g: Hebrew shabbat shabbaton, a sabbath of complete rest.

chapters.n: In future generations, whichever son succeeds as anointed high priest will perform this ritual in the linen garments.
Atonement covers everything: the Most Holy Place, the tent, the altar, the priests, and the whole congregation.

f.w: for all the people of the congregation

chapters.n: It is to happen once a year forever, and Moses and Aaron obey. Hebrews contrasts this yearly repetition with Christ’s single, eternal offering.
A new section begins. Many scholars call chapters 17–26 the “Holiness Code” because of its repeated call, “Be holy, for I am holy.”
This message is for everyone—priests and people alike. What follows concerns how all Israel handles the life of animals.
The law addresses anyone who slaughters an ox, lamb, or goat, whether inside or outside the camp.
Such animals must be brought to the tabernacle as offerings. Killing them elsewhere counted as shedding blood wrongly, and the person was to be cut off from the people.

f.w: blood shall be imputed unto that man
f.g: He is held guilty of bloodshed.

f.w: cut off from among his people
f.g: Removed from the covenant community; sometimes understood as a penalty God Himself carries out.

chapters.n: The goal is to bring worship that was happening “in the open field” to the Lord’s sanctuary, as peace offerings shared with God.
The priest handles the blood and fat properly at the altar, giving God His portion.

f.g: A pleasing aroma—an offering God accepts.

chapters.n: Some Israelites had been sacrificing to goat-demons in the wilderness. “Gone a whoring” pictures idolatry as unfaithfulness to a covenant marriage with God.

f.g: Hebrew se‘irim, “goat ones”—goat-demons or field spirits worshiped by neighboring peoples.

chapters.n: The rule for burnt offerings and sacrifices applies to foreigners living in Israel too.

f.g: Foreigners who live among Israel as residents.

chapters.n: Offering anywhere but the tabernacle meant being cut off. Worship was to be centered on the place God appointed.

f.w: bringeth it not unto the door

chapters.n: Eating blood is strictly forbidden. God says He will personally “set His face against” anyone who does it.

f.g: Turn in opposition to; a strong expression of divine judgment.

chapters.n: The key verse: life is in the blood, and God gave blood on the altar to atone. This is why the shedding of blood is central in sacrifice—and why Christ’s blood is so significant.

f.w: the life of the flesh is in the blood

chapters.n: Because blood stands for life given to God, no Israelite or foreigner among them may eat it.

f.w: No soul of you shall eat blood

chapters.n: Hunters must drain the blood of game and cover it with earth, treating it with respect.
The reason is repeated: blood is the life of all flesh. Life belongs to God, its Giver.
Eating an animal that died naturally or was killed by beasts causes uncleanness until evening, since its blood was not properly drained.

f.g: An animal found dead, not slaughtered.

chapters.n: Ignoring the washing brings guilt. Neglecting even small duties has consequences.

f.g: Be held responsible for his wrongdoing.

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses laws about sexual morality and family relationships—protecting marriage, family, and the vulnerable.
“I am the LORD your God” frames the whole chapter. These laws flow from Israel’s covenant relationship with Jehovah, not from mere custom.

f.w: I am the LORD your God

chapters.n: Israel must not imitate Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going. God’s people were to be distinct from surrounding cultures.
Instead, they are to follow God’s judgments and walk in His ways.
Keeping God’s laws leads to life. Paul quotes this verse; Nephi also taught that obedience brings life and blessing.
The general rule: no sexual relations with close relatives. “Uncover nakedness” is a polite Hebrew way of referring to sexual relations.
First prohibited: one’s own mother. Such a relationship would dishonor both father and mother.
A father’s wife (a stepmother) is also off limits, since it would dishonor the father. Paul condemns this very sin in Corinth.
Sisters and half-sisters are forbidden, whether raised in the same home or elsewhere.

f.w: born at home, or born abroad
f.g: Whether raised in the same household or elsewhere.

chapters.n: Granddaughters are forbidden, because they share the man’s own family flesh.
A half-sister through one’s father is still a sister and is forbidden.
An aunt on the father’s side is a close relative and forbidden.
An aunt on the mother’s side is likewise forbidden.
An uncle’s wife is treated as an aunt and is off limits.
A daughter-in-law is forbidden. Judah’s story with Tamar shows how serious this boundary was.
A brother’s wife is forbidden (the later levirate custom, where a man married his dead brother’s childless widow, was a special exception).
A man may not have relations with a woman and also her daughter or granddaughter. This is called “wickedness,” a strong moral word.

f.g: Hebrew zimmah, shameful or depraved conduct.

chapters.n: A man must not marry his wife’s sister while his wife lives, which would create rivalry and pain—as with Jacob, Leah, and Rachel.

f.g: To provoke her or make her a rival.

chapters.n: Relations during a woman’s monthly period are forbidden, connecting to the purity laws of chapter 15.
Adultery—relations with another man’s wife—is forbidden, as in the Ten Commandments.
Child sacrifice to Molech, a Canaanite god, is forbidden. Sacrificing children profaned God’s holy name.

f.g: A god of the Ammonites and Canaanites associated with child sacrifice.

chapters.n: Sexual relations between men are forbidden and called an “abomination,” something God finds deeply offensive. The Church continues to teach the law of chastity—sexual relations only within marriage between a man and a woman.

f.g: Hebrew to‘evah, something detestable to God.

chapters.n: Bestiality is forbidden for both men and women. It is “confusion”—a mixing of what God made distinct.

f.g: Hebrew tebel, a perversion of the natural order.

chapters.n: These practices defiled the nations God was driving out of Canaan.

f.w: which I cast out before you

chapters.n: The land itself is pictured as sickened by its inhabitants’ sins and “vomiting” them out. Moral corruption affects even the land.
Both Israelites and foreigners living among them must keep these standards.
A reminder in parentheses: these sins were why the former inhabitants lost the land.
A warning: if Israel does the same, the land will spit them out too—which later happened in the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles.

f.w: That the land spue not you out also

chapters.n: Individuals who commit these sins are to be cut off from the covenant people.
The chapter ends as it began: “I am the LORD your God.” Holiness is how Israel reflects whose people they are.

f.w: I am the LORD your God

chapters.n: The Lord speaks again to Moses. This chapter is one of the richest in Leviticus, showing that holiness touches every part of daily life.
The theme of the whole book: be holy because God is holy. Holiness means being set apart for God and becoming like Him. Peter quotes this verse.

f.g: Hebrew qadosh—set apart, distinct, belonging to God.

chapters.n: Respecting parents and keeping the Sabbath come first—echoing the Ten Commandments. Interestingly, mother is named before father here.

f.g: Here, to revere or deeply respect.

chapters.n: No idols or cast-metal gods. Worship belongs to the living God alone.

f.g: Idols made by pouring melted metal into molds.

chapters.n: Peace offerings are to be given willingly, in a way God accepts.

f.g: Voluntarily, so that it will be accepted for you.

chapters.n: The meat must be eaten within two days; leftovers on the third day are burned.
Eating it on the third day makes it unacceptable—sacred things have limits.
Doing so treats holy things carelessly, which brings guilt and being cut off.

f.g: Treated a sacred thing as ordinary.

chapters.n: Farmers must not harvest the edges of their fields or pick up what falls. The leftovers belong to the poor—a built-in welfare system.

f.g: Grain left behind by harvesters, which the poor could gather.

chapters.n: Vineyards too must not be stripped bare; some grapes are left for the poor and foreigners. Generosity was part of holiness.
No stealing, cheating, or lying—honesty in all dealings.
Swearing falsely by God’s name dishonors Him. Using His name to back up a lie was especially serious.
No defrauding or robbing. Day laborers must be paid the same day, since they depended on that wage to eat.

f.w: the wages of him that is hired

chapters.n: Do not take advantage of those who cannot hear or see. God sees what the deaf cannot hear and the blind cannot see, so “fear thy God.”

f.g: Something placed to make a person trip.

chapters.n: Judges must be fair—not favoring the poor out of pity or the powerful out of fear. True justice is impartial.
No gossiping or spreading slander, and no standing idly by when a neighbor’s life is in danger.

f.w: stand against the blood of thy neighbour
f.g: Endanger your neighbor’s life, or stand by while it is threatened.

chapters.n: Do not secretly hate others. Instead, speak to them honestly about a wrong so resentment does not grow and you do not share in their sin.
“Love thy neighbour as thyself”—Jesus called this the second great commandment. Holiness rules out revenge and grudges.
No mixing of animal breeds, seed types, or linen with wool. These rules likely taught Israel to respect God’s created order and to stay distinct.
If a man sleeps with a slave woman engaged to another man, there is punishment but not death, since she was not free to refuse. The law recognized her vulnerable status.

f.g: Here probably means an inquiry or punishment; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: The man must bring a ram as a guilt offering.
Through the offering he can be forgiven. The law offered a way back even after serious wrong.
Newly planted fruit trees are not harvested for three years—treated as “uncircumcised,” not yet dedicated. This also let trees mature.

f.g: Here meaning forbidden, not yet consecrated.

chapters.n: In the fourth year all the fruit is holy, given in thanks to God—a kind of firstfruits.
From the fifth year on, the owner may eat. Giving God the first brought the promise of greater increase.
No eating blood, and no fortune-telling or reading omens. Israel was to trust God rather than occult practices.

f.g: Look for good or bad omens; practice soothsaying.

chapters.n: No trimming hair or beards in certain styles—probably practices tied to pagan mourning or worship.

f.w: round the corners of your heads
f.g: Cut the hair at the temples, as some pagan rites did.

chapters.n: No cutting oneself for the dead or tattooing. The body was to be honored as God’s creation, not marked for pagan rites.

f.w: cuttings in your flesh for the dead

chapters.n: Fathers must never force daughters into prostitution—a practice linked to some pagan temples—or the land would fill with wickedness.
Keep the Sabbaths and reverence the sanctuary—holy time and holy space.
Do not consult mediums or spiritists. Seeking guidance from the dead or the occult defiles God’s people.

f.g: Wizards = those claiming secret knowledge; sorcerers.

chapters.n: Stand up in the presence of the elderly and honor them. Respect for age is tied to reverence for God.
Do not mistreat foreigners living among you.
Foreigners are to be treated like native-born Israelites and loved as oneself. Israel knew from Egypt what it felt like to be a stranger.

f.w: thou shalt love him as thyself

chapters.n: Honesty in business: no cheating with measuring tools of any kind.
Scales, weights, and dry and liquid measures must be accurate. The God who freed Israel from Egypt expects honest dealing.

f.g: A dry measure, roughly a bushel or a bit less.
A liquid measure, about a gallon (3–4 liters).

chapters.n: A closing call to obey all God’s statutes. The refrain “I am the LORD” appears again and again in this chapter, grounding every command in who God is.
Chapter 18 listed forbidden practices; this chapter sets the penalties for them. Ancient Israel was both a religious community and a nation with civil law.
Offering a child to Molech is punished by death, carried out by the community through stoning. Child sacrifice was among the worst crimes imaginable.
God Himself opposes such a person, because the act defiles His sanctuary and dishonors His name.

f.g: Treat God’s name as common or bring disgrace on it.

chapters.n: If the community looks the other way and does nothing about it...
...God will act against the man, his family, and all who join him. Silence in the face of evil makes people share responsibility.
Seeking out mediums and spiritists is also spiritual unfaithfulness, and God will cut such a person off.
The positive goal behind the penalties: sanctify yourselves and be holy.
God both commands holiness and is the one who makes Israel holy. Holiness is His gift as well as their effort.

f.w: I am the LORD which sanctify you

chapters.n: Cursing one’s parents—seriously dishonoring them—was a capital crime. Family respect was foundational to the covenant society.

f.w: curseth his father or his mother
his blood shall be upon him
f.g: He bears responsibility for his own death.

chapters.n: Adultery is punished by death for both the man and the woman—equal accountability.
Relations with a stepmother bring death for both people.
Relations with a daughter-in-law is called “confusion,” a perversion of family order.
Homosexual intercourse carried the death penalty under the law of Moses.
Marrying both a woman and her mother was punished by burning, possibly of the bodies after execution—a sign of the deep shame attached.
Bestiality was punished by death for the man, and the animal was killed too.
The same penalty applied to a woman. These laws treated men and women alike.
Relations between a brother and sister, including half-siblings, bring public disgrace and being cut off.

f.w: in the sight of their people

chapters.n: Relations during menstruation bring cutting off for both. Life-related blood was treated with special reverence.
Relations with an aunt bring guilt on both persons.
Relations with an uncle’s wife brings the penalty of dying childless—an especially heavy consequence in Israel, where descendants carried the family name.
Marrying a brother’s wife (while the brother lives, or outside the levirate custom) is also called unclean and brings childlessness.
Keeping these laws is how Israel will stay in the promised land.
Do not copy the nations being driven out; their deeds caused God to reject them.
Instead, Israel will inherit a rich land. God has set them apart from other peoples for a purpose.

f.g: A proverbial description of fertile, abundant land.

chapters.n: The food laws of chapter 11 were daily reminders that Israel was distinct. Separating clean from unclean animals taught them to separate holy from unholy.

f.w: put difference between clean beasts and unclean

chapters.n: A beautiful summary: God separated Israel “that ye should be mine.” Holiness is about belonging to God.
Mediums and spiritists themselves were to be executed. This closing verse returns to a danger named in verse 6.

f.g: One who claims secret knowledge; a sorcerer.

chapters.n: Now the Lord addresses the priests, Aaron’s sons. Touching a corpse caused ritual uncleanness, so priests were generally to avoid funerals.

f.g: Made ritually unclean by contact with a dead body.

chapters.n: An exception: a priest may become unclean to mourn his closest relatives—parents, children, and brother. God honored family grief.
He may also mourn an unmarried sister who still lived under his family’s care.
But as a leader he must not defile himself for others, such as relatives by marriage.

f.g: A leader; possibly “as a husband,” meaning for in-laws. The Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: Priests must not shave their heads, trim their beards, or cut their skin—mourning customs of pagan neighbors.
Because they offer “the bread of their God”—the sacrifices—priests must be holy. Their role represented God to the people.

f.g: A term for the offerings, pictured as food set before God.

chapters.n: A priest must not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman, since his household reflected his sacred role.

f.g: Here, a woman who has been defiled or dishonored.

chapters.n: Israel must treat the priest as holy because of his service, and God, who is holy, is the one who sanctifies them all.
A priest’s daughter who becomes a prostitute brings disgrace on her father; the penalty is death. The priest’s family was held to a higher standard.
The high priest, anointed and wearing the holy garments, has stricter rules. He must not show mourning by uncovering his head or tearing his clothes.

f.g: Tear one’s garments, a common sign of grief.

chapters.n: He may not approach any dead body—not even for his own parents. His duty to the living God came first.

f.w: go in to any dead body

chapters.n: He must not leave the sanctuary to mourn, because the holy anointing oil is like a crown upon him.

f.g: The anointing marked him as consecrated, like a crown marks a king.

chapters.n: The high priest must marry a virgin.
He may not marry a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, but only a young woman from Israel.
This protected the purity of the high priestly line, which God Himself sanctified.
A new instruction is given to Moses.
Descendants of Aaron with a physical defect may not offer sacrifices. Like the animals offered, the officiant was to be “without blemish”—a picture of perfection pointing to Christ.
Examples include blindness, lameness, or a disfigured face or limb.

f.g: Some disfigurement of the face; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Having a deformed or extra limb.

chapters.n: Also an injured foot or hand.
Also a hunched back, short stature, eye defects, skin diseases, or damaged reproductive organs.

f.g: Having a skin disease or rash, not the vitamin disease.

chapters.n: These men may not serve at the altar. The rule concerned outward symbolism in worship, not a person’s worth before God.
Yet they still eat the holy food and keep their priestly share. They remain fully part of the priestly family.

f.w: most holy, and of the holy
f.g: Two classes of priestly food from the offerings.
