chapters.n: Only service at the veil and altar is restricted. God’s concern was the visible symbolism of His sanctuary.
Moses passes the instructions on to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel—priestly rules were public knowledge.
The Lord continues instructions for the priests, now about the holy food they receive from offerings.
Priests must treat Israel’s holy offerings with care. Mishandling them would dishonor God’s name.

f.g: Keep a respectful distance, handling them only when properly clean.

chapters.n: Any priest who approaches holy things while unclean will be cut off from God’s presence. Sacred privileges require worthiness.
A priest with skin disease or a discharge may not eat holy food until healed. Nor may one who touched the dead or had an emission.
Touching unclean creatures or unclean people also disqualifies him for a time.

f.g: Small creatures such as lizards or rodents.

chapters.n: He stays unclean until evening and must bathe before eating holy food.
After sunset he is clean and may eat again, because this food is his livelihood.
Priests may not eat animals found dead or killed by wild beasts.
Priests who disregard these rules bring guilt—even death—on themselves. God is the one who makes them holy.

f.w: I the LORD do sanctify them

chapters.n: Outsiders—guests, temporary residents, or hired workers—may not eat holy food.

f.g: Here, anyone not of a priestly family.

chapters.n: But servants who permanently belong to the priest’s household, including those born there, may eat it. They were considered part of the family.
A priest’s daughter who marries outside the priestly line no longer eats holy food; she joins her husband’s household.
If she is widowed or divorced, childless, and returns home, she may eat again as a member of her father’s house. The law cared for vulnerable women.

f.g: As when she was young and lived at home.

chapters.n: Someone who eats holy food by accident must repay it plus a fifth more. Even unintentional wrongs were set right with restitution.
Priests must not let holy things be treated as common...
...nor allow people to bring guilt on themselves by eating them wrongly. Priests protected both the sacred and the people.
A new instruction about the quality of offerings.
Burnt offerings for vows or freewill gifts—from Israelites or resident foreigners—are addressed.

f.g: Voluntary gifts beyond what was required.

chapters.n: Such offerings must be males without blemish from cattle, sheep, or goats.
A defective animal is not acceptable. God deserves our best, not our leftovers. Malachi later rebuked priests for offering sick and lame animals.
Peace offerings for vows or freewill gifts must also be perfect. This foreshadows Christ, the Lamb “without blemish and without spot.”
No blind, injured, or diseased animals may be offered.

f.g: A wart, cyst, or running sore.

chapters.n: A small exception: an animal with a slightly malformed limb may be a freewill gift, but not fulfill a vow.

f.w: superfluous or lacking in his parts
f.g: With a limb too long or too short.

chapters.n: Animals with damaged reproductive organs may not be offered, and such practices were not to be done in Israel.

f.w: bruised, or crushed, or broken, or cut

chapters.n: Even defective animals bought from foreigners cannot be offered. The standard did not change based on the source.
Another instruction from the Lord.
Newborn animals stay with their mother seven days; from the eighth day they may be offered. The law showed tenderness even toward animals.
A mother and her young must not be killed on the same day—another sign of compassion built into the law.

f.w: her young both in one day

chapters.n: Thanksgiving sacrifices are to be offered willingly, in the right way.
The thanksgiving offering must be eaten the same day.

f.w: leave none of it until the morrow

chapters.n: Keep God’s commands and do them. Again the refrain: “I am the LORD.”
Do not profane God’s holy name; He will be honored as holy among His people. He is the one who makes them holy.
The basis for all these laws is redemption: God brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God. Obedience is a response to deliverance.

f.w: brought you out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: The Lord gives Moses Israel’s calendar of sacred times. These feasts shaped the rhythm of the year around remembering God.
These are “the feasts of the LORD”—His appointed times, not merely national holidays. A “holy convocation” was a sacred gathering for worship.
The weekly Sabbath comes first, the foundation of all holy time. It is to be kept in every home, not only at the sanctuary.
Now the yearly feasts, each to be announced in its season.
Passover is on the evening of the 14th of the first month (Abib, later called Nisan, in spring), remembering the night Israel was spared in Egypt. Jesus was crucified at Passover.
The seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread follows, recalling Israel’s hurried departure when there was no time for bread to rise.
The first day is a sacred assembly with no regular work.

f.g: Ordinary, laborious work; one’s regular occupation.

chapters.n: Offerings are made each of the seven days, and the last day is also a sacred assembly.
Another instruction from the Lord.
Once in Canaan, Israel was to bring the first sheaf of the barley harvest to the priest. Giving God the first acknowledged that the whole harvest came from Him.

f.g: A bundle of cut grain stalks.

chapters.n: The priest waves it before the Lord “on the morrow after the sabbath.” Christians have long noted that Christ rose on the day after the Sabbath as the “firstfruits” of the resurrection.

f.w: on the morrow after the sabbath

chapters.n: A perfect year-old lamb is offered as a burnt offering that day.
A grain offering and a wine drink offering go with it.

f.g: Tenths of an ephah of flour.
Wine poured out at the altar.
About a gallon; a fourth of a hin is roughly a quart.

chapters.n: No one may eat any of the new grain until the firstfruits have been offered. God came first, then the family table.

f.g: Roasted grain (“corn” in the KJV means grain, not maize).

chapters.n: From that day Israel counts seven full weeks.
On the fiftieth day comes a new grain offering. This feast is called Weeks or Pentecost (Greek for “fiftieth”), when the Holy Ghost was poured out in Acts 2.

f.g: Greek pentēkostē, “fiftieth,” gives the name Pentecost.

chapters.n: Two loaves of wheat bread, baked with leaven, are waved as firstfruits of the wheat harvest. Unusually, leavened bread is used here—ordinary daily bread offered to God.
Burnt offerings accompany the bread: seven lambs, a bull, and two rams, with grain and drink offerings.
A goat is offered for sin and two lambs as peace offerings.
The priest waves the bread and lambs before the Lord; they then belong to the priest.
Pentecost is also a sacred assembly with no regular work, a permanent ordinance.
Right in the middle of the feast calendar comes a reminder to leave the field edges for the poor. Joy in the harvest must include generosity.
Another instruction from the Lord.
The first day of the seventh month (autumn) is a day of rest marked by blowing trumpets (shofars). It is now known as Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year.

f.g: Probably ram’s-horn shofars; Hebrew teru‘ah, a trumpet blast or shout.

chapters.n: No regular work is done, and offerings are made.
Another instruction from the Lord.
Ten days later comes the Day of Atonement, described fully in chapter 16. The people humble themselves and offerings are made.
No work at all is done that day, for it is devoted to atonement before God.
Anyone who refuses to humble himself that day is cut off from the people.
Anyone who works on that day, God says, He will destroy from among the people. This was the most solemn day of the year.
A permanent law for all generations and all homes.
It is a sabbath kept from evening to evening, starting on the evening of the ninth. Israel’s days ran from sunset to sunset.
Another instruction from the Lord.
Five days after the Day of Atonement comes the joyful Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), lasting seven days.
Its first day is a sacred assembly with no regular work.
Offerings are made all seven days, and an eighth day closes the festival with a solemn assembly. Latter-day Saints may recall that the Kirtland Temple dedication included a solemn assembly.
A summary: these are the Lord’s feasts with their proper offerings, each on its day.
These are in addition to the weekly Sabbaths and to personal gifts, vows, and freewill offerings.
More detail on Tabernacles: it is kept after the fall harvest is gathered, with rest days on the first and eighth days.

f.w: gathered in the fruit of the land
f.g: So it is also called the Feast of Ingathering.

chapters.n: People gather branches of beautiful trees, palms, leafy trees, and willows and rejoice before the Lord for seven days. This was Israel’s happiest feast.
It is kept every year in the seventh month as a permanent ordinance.
Israelites live in temporary shelters (booths) for seven days.

f.g: Temporary shelters made of branches; Hebrew sukkot.

chapters.n: Living in booths helps each generation remember that God sheltered and cared for Israel in the wilderness. The feasts teach history through experience.
Moses announces the Lord’s feasts to the people.
The Lord gives Moses instructions about the daily care of the sanctuary’s lamps and bread.
The people supply the purest olive oil, pressed by beating rather than crushing, to keep the lamps burning continually. Light in God’s house was a shared offering.

f.g: The finest oil, from olives gently pounded rather than pressed.

chapters.n: Aaron tends the lamps from evening to morning in the Holy Place, just outside the veil that hid the ark.

f.g: The curtain before the ark, which held the tablets (“testimony”).

chapters.n: The lamps sit on the pure gold lampstand (menorah).

f.g: A lampstand with seven oil lamps—the menorah, not a candle holder.

chapters.n: Twelve loaves of fine flour are baked—one for each tribe of Israel. Each uses a large amount of flour.

f.g: Loaves; often called shewbread or “bread of the presence.”

chapters.n: They are set in two rows of six on the gold table before the Lord, representing all Israel continually in His presence.
Frankincense placed on each row is burned as a “memorial,” a reminder offered to God.

f.g: A fragrant resin burned as incense.

chapters.n: Fresh bread is set out every Sabbath as part of an everlasting covenant. Jesus later called Himself the Bread of Life.
The old loaves become holy food for the priests, eaten in the sanctuary. David once ate this bread in a time of need.

f.w: it shall be Aaron's and his sons'

chapters.n: The scene shifts to an event in the camp. A man with an Israelite mother and Egyptian father gets into a fight with an Israelite man.
During the fight he blasphemes—uses the Lord’s sacred name in a curse. He is brought to Moses. His mother is named, perhaps to show how such a family tragedy touches real people.

f.g: Spoke the divine name with contempt; Hebrew nqb, to pronounce or pierce.

chapters.n: He is kept in custody until God reveals what to do. Moses did not decide on his own but waited on revelation.

f.w: that the mind of the LORD might be shewed them

chapters.n: The Lord answers Moses.
The blasphemer is taken outside the camp. The witnesses lay hands on his head—placing responsibility back on him—and the community stones him.

f.w: lay their hands upon his head
f.g: A sign that the guilt of his words rests on him, not on those who heard.

chapters.n: A general rule follows: whoever curses God will bear the consequences.
Blasphemy of the Lord’s name carries the death penalty, for Israelites and foreigners alike. Jesus was later accused of blasphemy.

f.w: blasphemeth the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Murder is punished by death, a principle dating back to Noah.
Killing someone’s animal requires replacing it—restitution, not revenge.
If someone injures a neighbor, the penalty matches the injury.
“Eye for eye” limited punishment so it could not exceed the harm done; often it was settled by payment. Jesus taught His followers to go further and not seek revenge.

f.w: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
f.g: The principle of proportional justice (lex talionis).
breach = a fracture or broken bone

chapters.n: A summary: an animal is replaced, but a human life is sacred and murder is a capital crime.
The same law applies to native Israelites and foreigners—equal justice for all.
Moses relays God’s judgment and Israel carries it out. The story shows how seriously God’s holy name was to be treated.

f.w: did as the LORD commanded Moses

chapters.n: The setting is reaffirmed: the Lord speaks to Moses at Mount Sinai. These economic laws come with the same divine authority as the Ten Commandments.
In the promised land even the soil is to rest. The Sabbath principle extends from people to the land itself.
Farmers may work their fields and vineyards for six years.
The seventh year is a sabbatical year: no planting or pruning. Resting the land was an act of trust in God’s provision.

f.g: Cut back vines to improve growth.

chapters.n: Even crops that grow on their own are not harvested commercially that year.
Whatever grows naturally feeds everyone—owners, servants, hired workers, and foreigners alike. The sabbatical year leveled social differences.
Even livestock and wild animals share in what grows. God cares for all creation.
Seven sabbatical cycles, forty-nine years, are counted.
Then on the Day of Atonement a ram’s horn sounds across the land. Fittingly, liberty is announced on the day of reconciliation with God.

f.g: Hebrew shofar; “jubilee” comes from yobel, a ram’s horn.

chapters.n: The fiftieth year proclaims liberty to all: land returns to original families and people return home. These words are inscribed on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.

f.w: proclaim liberty throughout all the land

f.g: The fiftieth year of release and restoration.

chapters.n: Like the sabbatical year, the jubilee is a year without sowing or harvesting.
The jubilee is holy, and people eat directly from what the fields produce.
In the jubilee each person regains his family’s land. Poverty was never meant to be permanent in Israel.
In buying or selling land, no one should take advantage of another.
Land prices are based on how many years remain until the jubilee. In effect, one was buying a lease on the harvests, not the land itself.
More years left means a higher price; fewer years means a lower one. What is really sold is a number of harvests.
Fair dealing comes from fearing God. Economic honesty is a religious duty.
Obedience brings safety in the land.
The land will produce enough, and Israel will live securely.

f.w: the land shall yield her fruit

chapters.n: God anticipates the obvious worry: how will we eat if we do not plant?
His answer: He will send a triple harvest in the sixth year. Obedience requires faith that God will provide.
That bumper crop lasts until the new harvest comes in—a test and a blessing together.
The key principle: the land belongs to God; Israel are His tenants and guests. Latter-day revelation similarly teaches that the earth is the Lord’s and we are stewards.
Every land sale must allow for redemption—buying it back.

f.g: Buying back what was sold or lost.

chapters.n: If a poor man sells land, a close relative should buy it back for him. This relative is the “kinsman-redeemer,” like Boaz for Ruth—a powerful image of Christ the Redeemer.
If no relative can redeem it but the man later recovers financially...
...he may buy it back by paying for the remaining years until the jubilee.
If he cannot, the buyer keeps it until the jubilee, when it returns to the original family. The jubilee was a safety net no one could lose.
City houses inside walls follow different rules: the seller has one year to buy back his house.
After that year, the house belongs permanently to the buyer. City homes were not tied to the tribal land inheritance.
Village houses without walls are treated like farmland and return in the jubilee.
The Levites, who received no tribal territory, may always redeem their town houses.
Levite houses sold also return in the jubilee, since these towns were their only inheritance.
The pastureland around Levite towns may never be sold.
If a fellow Israelite becomes poor, support him so he can keep living among you—just as you would help a resident foreigner.
Do not charge interest on loans to the poor. Lending was meant to help, not to profit from someone’s hardship.
Do not lend money or food at interest.
God reminds Israel that He freed them and gave them the land. Those who received grace should give it.
If a fellow Israelite must sell himself to pay debts, do not treat him as a slave.
Treat him like a hired worker until the jubilee.
Then he and his children go free and return to their family land.
Israelites belong to God, who freed them from Egypt. They cannot be owned by others.
Do not rule over him harshly—as Pharaoh did to Israel.
The law permitted owning servants from surrounding nations. Ancient law regulated slavery, which was universal at the time; later scripture moves toward the dignity and freedom of all.
Servants could also be bought from foreign families living in the land.
These could be passed down. But Israelites must never rule harshly over one another.
If an Israelite sells himself to a wealthy foreigner living in Israel...
...he keeps the right to be redeemed by a relative.
An uncle, cousin, or other close relative may buy him back—or he may redeem himself if he can.
The price depends on the years left until the jubilee, figured as wages for a hired worker.
Many years left means paying more back.
Few years left means paying less.
Even while serving a foreigner he must be treated as a hired worker, not abused, with the community watching.

f.g: In your presence; the community is to make sure of it.

chapters.n: If not redeemed sooner, he and his children go free at the jubilee.
The chapter ends with the reason: Israel belongs to the Lord who redeemed them. Freedom is grounded in God’s ownership.

f.w: unto me the children of Israel are servants

chapters.n: The Lord opens this covenant chapter by restating the foundation: no idols of any kind. Worship belongs to Him alone.

f.g: A sacred pillar or standing stone used in pagan worship.

chapters.n: Keep the Sabbath and honor the sanctuary—holy time and holy place, the two pillars of Israel’s worship.
The blessings begin with a condition: “If ye walk in my statutes.” Covenant blessings follow obedience.

f.w: If ye walk in my statutes

chapters.n: Rain at the right time and abundant crops. In a land dependent on rainfall, this was life itself.
Harvests will be so large that threshing lasts until grape harvest, and grape harvest until planting time. Plenty and safety are promised.
Peace in the land: no fear, no dangerous animals, no invading armies.
Israel will defeat its enemies.
With God’s help a few will overcome many—an image of strength that comes from Him, not from numbers.

f.w: five of you shall chase an hundred

chapters.n: God will favor them, make them numerous, and keep His covenant—echoing His promises to Abraham.

f.w: make you fruitful, and multiply you

chapters.n: Harvests will be so abundant that old stored food must be cleared out to make room for the new.
The greatest blessing: God will dwell among them and never reject them. His presence is the heart of the covenant.
“I will walk among you”—like God walking with Adam in Eden. Paul quotes this promise for the Church.
God broke Israel’s yoke of slavery and let them walk upright—free people standing tall. A yoke was the wooden bar placed on oxen.

f.g: The straps of a yoke—a symbol of slavery.

chapters.n: Now the warnings: what will happen if Israel will not listen.
Rejecting God’s laws and breaking the covenant is described in strong terms—despising and loathing.
Disease, fever, and enemies stealing their crops will follow. These curses are the reverse of the blessings above.
God will turn against them; enemies will rule them, and they will run from shadows.
If they still do not listen, discipline will increase “seven times”—meaning complete, intensifying correction. The purpose is to turn them back.

f.g: A figure of full, thorough punishment.

chapters.n: Their pride will be broken. The sky will be like iron (no rain) and the ground like bronze (hard and barren).

f.w: heaven as iron, and your earth as brass

chapters.n: All their labor will produce nothing.
If they keep walking against God, more plagues will come.

f.g: Live in opposition to; be hostile toward.

chapters.n: Wild animals will kill children and livestock, and roads will be empty—a picture of a land falling apart.
If even this does not lead them to reform...
...God will “walk contrary” to them—treat them as they treat Him. The consequences match the choices.
Invading armies will come to enforce the broken covenant. When people crowd into walled cities, plague will strike.

f.w: avenge the quarrel of my covenant
f.g: Carry out the penalty for breaking the covenant.

chapters.n: Famine will be so severe that ten households share one oven and bread is rationed by weight.

f.g: The food supply that supports life, like a staff one leans on.

chapters.n: If they still refuse...
...God will discipline them in fury.
The horror of siege famine: parents eating their children. This tragically happened in the sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem, and among the Nephites.

f.w: ye shall eat the flesh of your sons

chapters.n: Their idolatrous shrines will be destroyed and their bodies cast down among their idols.

f.g: Hilltop shrines, often used for idol worship.

chapters.n: Cities and sanctuaries will be ruined; God will no longer accept their offerings.

f.g: The pleasing smell of offerings, a sign of acceptance.

chapters.n: The land will be so devastated that even the enemies settling there will be shocked.
Israel will be scattered among the nations. This prophecy was fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles and later dispersions; the Book of Mormon speaks often of this scattering.

f.w: I will scatter you among the heathen

chapters.n: While Israel is in exile, the land will finally get the sabbath rests they neglected to give it.
The land rests because Israel had not let it rest.
Survivors in exile will be so fearful that a rustling leaf sends them running.

f.g: A vivid image of panic and lost courage.

chapters.n: They will stumble over each other fleeing from no one, unable to stand against enemies.
Many will perish in foreign lands.
Those left will waste away because of their own sins and their ancestors’ sins.
But there is hope: if they confess their sins and their fathers’ sins and acknowledge their rebellion...

f.w: If they shall confess their iniquity

chapters.n: ...and humble their hard hearts and accept the consequences...

f.g: Hearts not dedicated to God; stubborn hearts.

chapters.n: ...then God will remember His covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham, and the land. The covenant with the fathers is the ground of Israel’s gathering.
The land will rest while empty, and the people will accept their punishment for having rejected God’s ways.
Even in exile, God will not abandon or utterly destroy them, nor break His covenant. This promise underlies the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.w: I will not cast them away

chapters.n: God will remember the covenant made with the generation He brought out of Egypt before the eyes of the nations.
A closing statement: these are the laws God gave through Moses at Sinai. Chapter 27 forms an appendix.
A closing appendix to Leviticus: the Lord gives rules for voluntary vows and for tithes.
Sometimes a person vowed to dedicate themselves or a family member to God. Since only Levites served at the sanctuary, the vow was usually fulfilled by paying a set value.
An adult man aged 20–60 is valued at fifty silver shekels, measured by the sanctuary’s standard weight. The values reflect a person’s typical working capacity, not their worth to God.

f.g: The official standard weight used at the tabernacle; a shekel was roughly 11–12 grams of silver.

chapters.n: A woman of the same age is valued at thirty shekels, reflecting differences in typical labor value in that economy.
Young people from 5 to 20 years are valued at twenty shekels for a male and ten for a female.
Children from one month to five years are valued at five or three shekels.
Those over sixty are valued at fifteen or ten shekels. Interestingly, the gap between men and women narrows with age.
A compassionate exception: if the person is too poor, the priest sets a price he can afford. No one is shut out of making a vow to God by poverty.
An animal suitable for sacrifice that is vowed to God becomes holy—it now belongs to Him.
It cannot be swapped for another. If someone tries, both animals become holy. The rule discouraged second thoughts after a promise to God.

f.w: a good for a bad, or a bad for a good
f.g: Substituting a better or worse animal.

chapters.n: An unclean animal, which could not be sacrificed, is brought to the priest for appraisal.

f.g: An animal not fit for sacrifice, such as a donkey or camel.

chapters.n: The priest’s valuation is final.
To buy it back, the owner adds a fifth (20 percent) to the price. The extra discouraged casual reversals of a vow.
A house dedicated to God is appraised by the priest, whatever its condition.

f.g: Dedicate as holy, give to God.

chapters.n: The owner may buy it back for the value plus a fifth.
Dedicated farmland is valued by the amount of seed needed to plant it: fifty shekels for a homer of barley seed.

f.g: A large dry measure, roughly a donkey-load (perhaps 200 liters).

chapters.n: If dedicated starting in the jubilee year, the full price applies.
If dedicated later, the price drops according to the years left until the next jubilee, since the land would return then.
The owner can redeem the field by paying the value plus a fifth.
If he does not redeem it, or sells it to someone else, he loses the right to redeem it.
At the jubilee such a field becomes permanently holy, belonging to the priests.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem, irrevocably given to God.

chapters.n: Purchased land, which was not part of someone’s family inheritance, could also be dedicated.
Its value is calculated up to the jubilee, and the money is paid that day.
At the jubilee it returns to the original family owner. A person could only give what was truly theirs.
All values use the sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs.

f.g: A gerah was a small weight, one-twentieth of a shekel.

f.w: twenty gerahs shall be the shekel

chapters.n: Firstborn animals already belong to God, so they cannot be “given” as a vow.
An unclean firstborn animal may be redeemed for its value plus a fifth, or else it is sold.
Something “devoted” (ḥerem) is wholly God’s and can never be sold or bought back. It is most holy.

f.g: Something permanently and completely given to God.

chapters.n: A person placed under ḥerem—usually under God’s judgment, such as in war or for idolatry—could not be redeemed but was put to death. This is difficult law from an ancient setting.
A tenth of all crops and fruit belongs to the Lord and is holy. Tithing goes back to Abraham and is reaffirmed in latter-day revelation.
A person could redeem part of his crop tithe by paying its value plus a fifth.
A tenth of livestock is holy too. As animals passed under the shepherd’s rod to be counted, every tenth was set apart.

f.g: Animals were counted one by one as they passed beneath a shepherd’s staff.

chapters.n: The owner may not pick and choose which animal is tenth; swapping makes both holy. Tithing is honest and impartial.
Leviticus closes by reminding readers these commandments came from the Lord to Moses at Sinai for Israel.
